intro.title: Some things are worth coming home to.
intro.1: The office windows held a hundred small reflections of the same tired evening. Then a cream envelope slipped beneath your door. It smelled faintly of cedar.
intro.2: My dear one, I am finally taking that long train ride. The farm is yours, if you would like it. The roof grumbles, and the orchard has opinions. Look after the valley and the tree. Begin with something small. Love, Wren.
intro.3: By morning, the city was behind you. By evening, a cart rounded a bend and there it was: a little valley, a crooked gate, a place that did not yet know your name.
intro.4: “You must be Wren’s family.” Odalie tucked a growing stack of papers beneath her arm. “We have rather a lot to talk about. But first, let us get you home.”

guide.title: A small field guide
guide.farming: Clear weeds with the sickle, stones with the hammer, and branches with the axe. Till with the hoe. Choose your seeds, sow, then water. Rain does the watering for you.
guide.growth: Crops count watered nights, not calendar days. Turnips need four. Hold your tool key to charge an upgraded tool. Harvest with your hands; the shipping bin pays you overnight.
guide.community: Say hello every day. Each neighbor accepts one gift per day, two each week. The journal keeps your story goals, and the calendar remembers birthdays.
guide.rest: Your bed is in the farmhouse. Rest before midnight to recover fully. Save at the diary, or export a backup from the menu. Morning autosaves look after the start of each day.
guide.controls: WASD / arrows: walk. Space / Z: interact. Q / E: cycle tools. I: bag. J: journal. Esc: menu. Shift: run. Touch and gamepad controls are supported.
guide.paths: Use the paths and doors to explore. The valley map shows connected destinations. The riverside has livestock and building supplies; Market Lane has seeds, the forge, and the inn.

festival.cartHelp: Build a six-flower cart: choose at least three flower colors and mirror the arrangement from left to right. Use buttons or keys 1–4. Enter submits.
festival.feastHelp: Set six dishes along the table. Include all four kinds, and alternate neighboring dishes so everyone can reach something different. Keys 1–4 choose; Enter serves.
festival.judgeHelp: Choose a crop or animal from your farm for judging. Crop quality, animal affection, feeding, and brushing matter. If your farm is new, share a small garden display. Enter submits.
festival.memoryHelp: Watch the six numbered lights, then repeat the sequence with buttons or keys 1–4. Replay the lights whenever you need.
festival.lanternHelp: Choose a companion, then release a lantern as the marker reaches gold. Tap the button or Space once per crossing. Ten lanterns carry your wishes.
festival.emberHelp: Follow the numbered forest markers. Press the glowing number, or its key 1–4, when the moving marker crosses gold. Ten steps lead you home.
festival.bloomHelp: The four candles sing in turn. Press the glowing candle, or its key 1–4, as the marker reaches gold. Keep the harmony through ten notes.
festival.kiteHelp: Lift your kite with the shore breeze. Press Space or the button when the marker passes through gold. One lift per crossing; ten breezes in all.
festival.gentle: Another gentle chance on the next crossing.

dialogue.text: The council clock is six minutes fast. I regard that as a personal criticism.
Welcome. Sit down. No, that chair contains petitions. Take mine.
I have scheduled a quiet afternoon. Already three people have complained about it.
There are seventeen keys on this ring. Only eight doors remain in town.
A village needs more than a balanced ledger. Unfortunately, it needs that too.
If you find my blue pencil, it has been conducting independent inspections.
Please sign the attendance sheet. Your presence counts even without a speech.
I promised to listen before I answered. It is harder than it sounds.
The square belongs to everyone, including people who dislike my flower choices.
I know how the vote looks. I am still glad you came.
I keep Wren’s letters under the emergency forms. They work better.
A new farmer means another person asking why Tuesday has so many meetings.
Do eat before repairing the entire valley. I tried the reverse.
Our oldest bylaw concerns geese. Our newest also concerns geese.
You may disagree with me without making an appointment.

Corran: Not today. Another time, perhaps.
You stay until his tea cools.

heartEvents.title: The Photograph
lines: Corran opens his chest without looking away from you.
Inside is a photograph of a younger Lira holding an enormous fish.
Corran: She insisted it smiled.
He laughs, then finds the older map beneath it.
The room contains joy and fear without asking either to leave.
He keeps the chest open after showing you.

heartEvents.title: The Escaping Washer
lines: A washer rolls between the dock boards.
Lira watches it fall into the water.
Lira: That was the expensive splash.
You help lay a cloth beneath the next repair.
Lira: Less heroic than diving, much more useful.
The remaining washers stay where both of you can reach them.

heartEvents.title: A Useful Mistake
lines: Lira shows you two practice seams.
One leaks at the edge.
Lira: I made that one too quickly to impress Granddad.
She marks the fault before starting again.
You hold the timber while she checks the fit.
Lira: I prefer somebody who will stay for the repair.

heartEvents.title: Past the Mooring Post
lines: Lira sits beside you with a coil of finished rope.
Lira: I keep planning where to go.
She glances toward the village lights.
Lira: Lately I also plan who I want to come back to.
The coil rests between your hands.
Neither of you reaches to put it away.

heartEvents.title: Permission for a Sketch
lines: Sable lifts a sketchbook, then lowers it.
Sable: May I draw your hands?
You hold them where the light reaches.
The drawing keeps the dirt beneath one thumbnail.
Sable: I didn’t want to make them less yours.
You recognize your own work in the lines.

heartEvents.title: The Name on the Back
lines: Sable has signed a painting where nobody will see it.
You turn the canvas gently.
Sable: Signing the front feels like taking up space.
The town hall wall has room to spare.
Sable adds a small clear name in the corner.
You stand beside the painting while the ink dries.

heartEvents.title: The Furnished Silence
lines: Two chairs face the window in Sable’s cottage.
Sable: I moved the boxes before I invited you.
You sit while the light changes across an unfinished canvas.
There is nothing either of you has to prove.
Sable: This silence feels like a room now.
A kettle begins to sing in the next corner.

heartEvents.title: The Returned Book
lines: A package arrives without a return address.
Inside is a book borrowed nineteen years ago.
Fenwick checks its cover before the ledger.
Fenwick: Well. Welcome back.
He cancels the fine before writing a small note inside.
The collection is larger by one returned possibility.

heartEvents.title: A Useful Margin
lines: Fenwick shows you a ledger of bridge expenses.
Between two totals is a sketch of a sleeping dog.
Fenwick: The treasurer’s dog, according to his daughter.
The official record seems suddenly inhabited.
You help preserve the fragile page.
Fenwick labels the sketch as carefully as the accounts.

heartEvents.title: The Reader’s Chair
lines: A chair has been moved closer to the low shelves.
Fenwick says a child suggested it.
Fenwick: An excellent review of our facilities.
You test the reach and find a favorite book easily.
He writes down the change in the library log.
History can include an improvement made on an ordinary afternoon.

heartEvents.title: The Quiet Hive
lines: Hollis raises one hand before opening a hive.
Hollis: Listen first.
The sound changes as he tilts the lid.
He explains what the colony is telling him.
You wait while a bee crosses your glove.
For once, his lesson contains no argument.

heartEvents.title: The Uncut Hedge
lines: The hedge blocks half the path to the shed.
Hollis holds the shears without using them.
Hollis: Our parents planted it.
You point out the new shoots beneath the old growth.
He cuts a careful opening instead of removing the hedge.
Memory remains, with room to walk through.

heartEvents.title: The Missing Expense
lines: Hollis shows you his meticulous farm ledger.
A whole season contains no allowance for his own rest.
He notices where your finger stops.
Hollis: I didn’t know how to enter that.
You help him make a new column.
The first blank square looks like space rather than failure.

heartEvents.title: The Beetle’s Lesson
lines: June tries to begin a lesson on maps.
A beetle walks across the page.
The children ask where it believes it is going.
June puts down the planned worksheet.
Together you draw a map from the beetle’s height.
The lesson ends with six new questions.

heartEvents.title: The Letter Without Always
lines: June reads a letter she has revised several times.
Every crossed-out sentence began with you always.
June: It sounds less impressive now.
You tell her it sounds easier to answer.
She adds one question about the farm.
The envelope is closed before she can rewrite the whole thing.

heartEvents.title: A Place at School
lines: June sets a small chair beside the classroom door.
June: For a child who needs a moment without leaving altogether.
You help smooth a splinter on its arm.
Later, a child sits there and returns to the lesson alone.
June smiles without calling attention to it.
The chair has done its quiet work.

heartEvents.title: The Unsymbolic Leak
lines: A bowl catches water beneath the chapel roof.
Ilse: Before you ask, this represents a hole.
You carry another bowl while she fetches a ladder.
The repair takes less time than a solemn interpretation.
Afterward you share tea in the dry corner.
Ilse: A useful ceremony, I think.

heartEvents.title: A Candle for Nobody
lines: Ilse lights a small candle beside an empty chair.
Ilse: Someone may come. They may not.
You ask whether that feels wasteful.
She watches the flame settle.
Ilse: So little light, to make room before a person has to ask.
You sit in the next chair for a while.

heartEvents.title: The Keeper’s Joke
lines: Ilse tells you a joke so ordinary you laugh in surprise.
Ilse: Did you expect it to involve four seasons?
The Lantern Tree drops a leaf into her tea.
She looks at it with dignified disappointment.
Ilse: Apparently the tree prefers symbolism.
You help find a clean cup.

heartEvents.title: A Real Job
lines: Pip has been asked to carry a basket with nothing in it.
Pip: That isn’t helping. That’s holding.
You put the light seed labels inside.
Pip carries them carefully to the right table.
Each label goes beside a real tray.
The empty basket returns with a very proud owner.

heartEvents.title: The Longer Shortcut
lines: Pip leads you along a supposed shortcut.
It takes twice as long as the main path.
At the bend, a beetle crosses a fallen branch.
Pip: See? That’s what the other path misses.
You watch it reach the far end.
The longer walk has delivered exactly what was promised.

heartEvents.title: Three Figures
lines: Pip draws three people beside the bee shed.
The middle figure holds both the others’ hands.
Pip: Is it cheating if I draw what I want?
You find a place for the picture where everyone can see it.
Pip adds a fourth cup for a visitor.
There is room on the paper without erasing anyone.

heartEvents.title: The Practical Compartment
lines: Ozzie opens a hidden compartment with magnificent ceremony.
Inside are dry socks.
Ozzie: A traveler’s most underrated treasure.
A sudden shower makes the demonstration persuasive.
He gives you a pair to keep your walk comfortable.
The mystery ends usefully.

heartEvents.title: An Object’s Honest Story
lines: A customer asks whether a box is truly ancient.
Ozzie studies the freshly cut hinge.
Ozzie: No. It is quite young and rather well made.
The customer buys it anyway.
Afterward he looks almost surprised.
Ozzie: A respectable story can stand on its own feet.

heartEvents.title: A Return Date
lines: Ozzie checks the road map beneath his cart lamp.
One route could keep him away for months.
He marks Willowmere on the return loop.
Ozzie: Business, naturally.
Then he asks whether you will be here for supper that day.
You help him write the date clearly on the notice board.

heartEvents.title: The Case on the Bench
lines: Halverd sets his leather case beneath the bench.
For once, he does not open it when you approach.
Halverd: I was trying to remember the name of our old baker.
You sit while he searches his memory.
The name returns with the smell of warm bread.
His next sentence contains no financial term.

heartEvents.title: The Unused Bandstand
lines: Halverd shows you a photograph from his hometown.
The report beside it calls the bandstand idle infrastructure.
Halverd: My father played there every Sunday.
You ask who decided it was idle.
He looks at the phrase for a long time.
Then he crosses it out.

heartEvents.title: A Smaller Map
lines: Halverd’s new map shows a footpath in unusual detail.
Halverd: The family at the end uses it for deliveries.
He has measured the gentle slope as well as the distance.
You walk the route with him.
At the far gate, he puts the map away before greeting the resident.
The survey has acquired a face.

heartEvents.title: The Familiar Kettle
lines: Wren lifts the kettle and checks the old repair.
Wren: Still holding. Greta pretended that wasn’t a favor.
You make tea in the kitchen she left behind.
She notices the things you have changed.
Wren: Good. I wanted to give you a place, not preserve mine.
She sits in the chair you offer.

heartEvents.title: A Story with the Other Half
lines: Wren listens while Corran tells the rescue story.
When he reaches the rope, she raises a hand.
Wren: Tell them who pulled me back.
Corran looks toward the water, then begins that part.
The story becomes less tidy and more generous.
Lira listens without needing either of them to be fearless.

heartEvents.title: Permission to Travel
lines: Wren watches you finish the evening watering.
Wren: If you ever want to see a little road, I can mind this.
She quickly adds that staying is also a fine choice.
You stand where the orchard path meets the gate.
Wren: I am learning to offer company without writing the journey.
The gate opens easily in either direction.

heartEvents.title: The Window Table
lines: Ivy has cleared the small table by the bakery window.
Two plates wait beside a test pastry.
Ivy: This isn’t customer research.
She blushes and leaves the phrase where it is.
You share the pastry while the store bell rings beyond the door.
For once, she lets the next batch wait a few minutes.

heartEvents.title: A Recipe in Two Hands
lines: Ivy brings a recipe with the last line blank.
Ivy: I know the filling. I don’t know what we’ll call it.
You cook together, tasting and adjusting.
The kitchen grows warm enough to open a window.
She writes both your initials beneath the recipe.
Ivy: We can change it next time. There will be a next time.

heartEvents.title: The Ordinary Morning
lines: Ivy arrives with breakfast wrapped in a clean cloth.
Ivy: I used to imagine love as something that interrupted life.
She hands you the warmest roll.
Ivy: Lately I imagine making enough breakfast for two.
The river carries the early light past your feet.
Her hand finds yours without hurrying the answer.

heartEvents.title: The Quiet Seat
lines: Kip has put a cushion on the paddock bench.
Kip: I thought you might come.
The words surprise him by arriving without practice.
You sit while the animals settle in the evening grass.
His shoulder rests lightly against yours.
Neither of you moves away from the comfortable space.

heartEvents.title: A Lead with Room
lines: Kip walks beside you with the ranch dog on a loose lead.
Kip: Trust isn’t holding so tightly nothing can move.
He looks embarrassed by his own seriousness.
You take his free hand.
The dog pauses to inspect a leaf with great importance.
Kip has time to smile before the walk continues.

heartEvents.title: Something Worth Saying
lines: Kip has written a sentence on a scrap of feed paper.
He folds it before you can read.
Kip: I wanted to say this without checking.
He takes a breath.
Kip: I like the life I imagine when you’re in it.
The paper stays folded in his pocket.

heartEvents.title: The Piano Afternoon
lines: Ansel sits at the piano without his clinic coat.
His first chord is uncertain.
You listen while his hands remember the next one.
Ansel: I used to think I had to be useful every minute.
He leaves room on the bench beside him.
The afternoon becomes useful in a way no chart measures.

heartEvents.title: No Appointment Needed
lines: Ansel arrives exactly on time and apologizes for that too.
Then he laughs at himself.
Ansel: I am learning how to come simply because I want to.
You walk without discussing work until he chooses to.
He asks about the thing that made you happy today.
The answer has room to be small.

heartEvents.title: A Sustainable Kind of Love
lines: Ansel pauses beneath the branches.
Ansel: I want to care for you without turning you into someone I must manage.
He asks what support feels like to you.
The conversation takes time and several honest pauses.
You find a way of holding hands that leaves both of you comfortable.
There is no appointment waiting at the end of the path.

heartEvents.title: The Dry Seat
lines: Lira has covered one seat in the boat with a clean cloth.
Lira: I promised the least spray, not absolute luxury.
The tide is gentle enough for a short sheltered trip.
You return before the evening wind rises.
Lira keeps the mooring line loose while you climb out.
Lira: I like a journey that ends with another invitation.

heartEvents.title: Two Shores
lines: Lira lays a map between your supper dishes.
It marks both a distant harbor and the farm.
Lira: I don’t want choosing you to mean choosing a smaller world.
You talk about journeys, work, and coming home.
She adds a little path between two places on the map.
Lira: We can keep drawing it.

heartEvents.title: The Return Knot
lines: Lira shows you the knot she uses when she expects to return soon.
It holds securely without fighting the hands that open it.
Lira: There’s a lesson in that, but Ilse charges by the metaphor.
She laughs, then takes your hand.
Lira: I want to come back to you.
The tide lifts the boat gently against its line.

heartEvents.title: The Unpainted Afternoon
lines: Sable arrives without a sketchbook.
Sable: I kept turning good moments into work so I could keep them.
You watch the changing valley light together.
There is no record except what each of you remembers.
Sable leans a little closer.
Sable: Perhaps being in the picture is enough today.

heartEvents.title: A Portrait Asked For
lines: Sable turns a covered canvas toward you.
Sable: You may tell me what doesn’t feel right.
The portrait shows you resting, not working.
You talk about the expression before the color.
Sable changes one line and leaves another.
The painting becomes a conversation neither of you has to win.

heartEvents.title: A Place in the Frame
lines: Sable sets a small frame on the bench.
It contains two pressed leaves, gathered on different walks.
Sable: They weren’t beautiful in the same way.
A hand reaches for yours beside the frame.
Sable: I like the space they make together.
The square feels familiar enough to stay in after sunset.

arcEvents.title: The Envelope
lines: Marta flattens a letter beside the flour bin.
Marta: Halverd’s company bought the debt.
Marta: I kept serving supper because supper was something I could finish.
You read the repayment date together.
Marta: I need ingredients for a fundraiser. And somebody who knows the truth.

arcEvents.title: A Table to Fill
lines: Baskets arrive at the kitchen door.
Ivy labels the loaves with the growers’ names.
Marta: I thought charity would make this place smaller.
Noor: Fair payment and shared work are not charity.
Marta puts another apron on the hook.

arcEvents.title: The Mayor’s Chair
lines: Odalie studies the inn’s accounts.
Odalie: The inn shelters visitors and neighbors. That is a public service.
Marta: I want help, not a ceremonial ribbon over the debt.
Odalie: Then let us write something useful.
A support plan goes onto the council agenda.

arcEvents.title: More Than One Key
lines: The fundraiser fills the dining room.
Marta lays two plans on the table.
One keeps her as innkeeper with a sustainable village loan.
The other places ownership in a village co-op, with Marta leading the kitchen.
Marta: Tell me which future you would help carry.

arcEvents.title: An Open Door
lines: Bram repairs the porch while the new agreement dries.
Marta hangs a second set of keys beside the first.
Marta: Saved is a lovely word. Shared is the one that will last.
Dex tests a chord in the dining room.
The inn opens for supper with flowers on every table.

arcEvents.title: The Timetable
lines: A timetable slips from Dex’s music book.
Dex: I applied for a room near a music hall.
Dex: Mum thinks I am checking delivery routes.
He folds the paper along a well-used crease.
Dex: I wish wanting more did not feel like an insult.

arcEvents.title: A Song with No Ending
lines: Dex plays a melody and stops before its final phrase.
Dex: Every ending sounds like choosing.
You listen while he tries a quieter chord.
Dex: Perhaps I need to decide who the song belongs to.
He writes his own name at the top.

arcEvents.title: Permission to Want
lines: Marta sets a cup beside the timetable.
Marta: You don’t have to make me stop loving this place to love another.
Dex: And if I stay?
Marta: Make something you want to stay for.
Dex looks toward the little piano.

arcEvents.title: Two Good Roads
lines: Dex has a city invitation and a plan for music nights.
Dex: I want your honest thought, not a vote on whether I love home.
The city offers lessons and unfamiliar rooms.
The inn offers a stage he can build himself.
Dex: Either road will need courage.

arcEvents.title: A Door That Opens Both Ways
lines: Dex puts the inn key on a fresh cord.
Dex: A key can mean coming back as well as staying.
He plays the finished song for the supper crowd.
Marta listens without checking the kitchen once.
The last chord leaves room for applause.

arcEvents.title: The Spare Gloves
lines: Hollis finds June’s gloves in the bee shed.
Hollis: She left these and everything else for me to carry.
Pip: She sent books.
Hollis sets the gloves down carefully.
The old argument has more than one inventory.

arcEvents.title: Two Letters
lines: June shows you a letter she never sent.
June: I wrote about being allowed to leave. I forgot to ask what staying cost him.
Hollis’s reply, also unsent, lists roof repairs and winter losses.
Neither letter says I miss you.
Both mean it.

arcEvents.title: At the Hives
lines: June arrives with the spare veil.
Hollis shows her where the hive entrance moved.
June: You kept them well.
Hollis: You learned things I don’t know.
For a few minutes, work gives them a shared language.

arcEvents.title: Family Honey
lines: At Harvest Scales, Pip unfolds a sign.
It reads FAMILY HONEY in enormous careful letters.
June offers to handle records and two weekly hive rounds.
Hollis admits he needs the help.
They ask whether to share ownership or keep ownership separate with a written work agreement.

arcEvents.title: Three Places
lines: Three cups stand on the kitchen table.
Pip puts the prize ribbon beside a jar that did not win.
Hollis: We can review the plan after winter.
June: Together.
The spare gloves hang beside the working pair.

arcEvents.title: Cold Tea
lines: Ansel reaches for a cup and finds yesterday’s tea.
Ansel: I am fine. That was too quick an answer, wasn’t it?
A patient waits while he checks a simple instruction twice.
Ansel sets the chart down.
Ansel: I need to change something before tired becomes unsafe.

arcEvents.title: An Empty Square
lines: The weekly rota has no blank afternoon.
Ansel: I thought availability was the same as care.
Marta arrives with contact details for a neighboring doctor.
Marta: Good care can have more than one name.
Ansel drafts a request for cover.

arcEvents.title: The Handover
lines: The substitute’s letter asks clear practical questions.
Ansel lists supplies, ongoing cases, and emergency contacts.
Ansel: Writing down what I don’t know is harder.
You help prepare the waiting room notice.
The clinic will remain open while he rests.

arcEvents.title: A Walk Without the Bag
lines: Ansel reaches automatically for his medical bag.
Then he leaves it on the clinic desk.
Ansel: Would you prefer a quiet walk or company at the piano?
If you are dating, his hand rests beside yours without a question about symptoms.
For once, the afternoon has no appointment after it.

choices.label: Spend an afternoon at the piano

arcEvents.title: A Sustainable Promise
lines: The new rota hangs where everyone can read it.
Ansel closes the clinic on time.
Ansel: I still care. I am beginning to believe rest proves that.
He takes a music book from the drawer.
The waiting room plant no longer has the healthiest schedule in the building.

arcEvents.title: From the Doorway
lines: Sable sketches the square from behind a post.
Sable: I don’t want to take up anyone’s space.
Pip leans around the post.
Pip: There’s more space over here.
Sable steps into the light.

arcEvents.title: Permission to Look
lines: Greta studies the sketch of her tools.
Greta: You left the worn handle in.
Sable: It seemed important.
Greta sits for a portrait on the condition she may see it first.
Sable writes that promise on the back.

arcEvents.title: The Empty Wall
lines: Odalie offers the town hall’s longest wall.
Sable: That is a frightening amount of welcome.
Bram measures for hooks.
Odalie: Start with one picture, then decide on the next.
The first hook goes in.

arcEvents.title: Names Beside Faces
lines: The portraits wait beneath clean cloths.
Sable asks whether the labels should use memories or short interviews.
Either choice lets the subjects speak alongside the painter.
Sable: I want people to recognize themselves, not only my brush.
A low section is reserved for children’s pictures.

arcEvents.title: Opening
lines: The village gathers before the uncovered portraits.
Greta stands before hers longer than she intends.
Pell points out Noor’s laughing eyes.
Sable signs the final label in clear dark letters.
Sable: Thank you for letting me learn how to stay.

arcEvents.title: The Flour Plan
lines: Ivy spreads a flour-marked plan over the counter.
Ivy: The side room could hold an oven and two cooling racks.
Pell begins listing what might go wrong.
Noor asks to hear what might go right first.
Ivy takes a steadying breath.

arcEvents.title: Three Trial Loaves
lines: Three trial loaves cool beside a bowl of harvest ingredients.
One is too dense; one splits; one draws a small crowd.
Ivy records all three results.
Noor: Include the time you worked.
Ivy writes a wage into the margin.

arcEvents.title: The Family Meeting
lines: Pell brings an oven estimate of his own.
Pell: I have been measuring when you weren’t here.
Ivy: I need you to trust the plan, not protect me from having one.
Noor reads the figures aloud.
They agree to a trial opening with clear responsibilities.

arcEvents.title: A Name on the Door
lines: Ivy holds two sign sketches.
One presents the bakery as part of the family store.
The other gives her counter its own name and entrance sign.
Ivy: Both can work. I want to choose how people find me.
Pell promises to hang whichever she selects.

choices.label: Give the bakery its own sign

arcEvents.title: The First Morning
lines: The oven door opens without sticking.
Ivy places the first tray beneath the new sign.
Noor rings up a loaf and hands Ivy the coin.
Pell waits in line instead of reaching across the counter.
Ivy: Good morning. What would you like?

arcEvents.title: The Announcement
lines: Rosalind offers Kip the animal-show list.
Kip reads the names without difficulty until he imagines the crowd.
Kip: Couldn’t someone else speak?
Rosalind: Certainly. I am asking whether you would like to learn.
Kip keeps the list.

arcEvents.title: A Patient Audience
lines: Kip practices while you hold the show board.
A cow interrupts exactly where he loses his place.
He laughs and starts again.
Kip: Maybe I can pause without apologizing.
The second attempt is slower and clearer.

arcEvents.title: The Small Job
lines: A child cannot settle a nervous lamb.
Kip kneels, explains the lead, and waits.
The lamb steps forward.
Rosalind: That was a demonstration, dear.
Kip realizes several people were listening.

arcEvents.title: A Voice That Fits
lines: Kip prepares the show program.
He can lead the whole introduction or share it with Rosalind.
Kip: Sharing it wouldn’t mean I failed, would it?
Rosalind: It would mean you organized a show.
He chooses a plan he can practice.

arcEvents.title: Welcome to the Show
lines: Kip stands on the steady platform.
Kip: Welcome. We’ll give every animal time to settle.
The crowd does exactly that.
His voice is quiet, and everybody hears it.
Afterward he folds the speech and puts it away.

arcEvents.title: The Hull on Blocks
lines: Lira taps a split seam with a pencil.
Lira: This is a boat if we do the work. Otherwise it is optimistic firewood.
She lists wood, iron fittings, and dry time.
Corran watches from the pier.
Lira leaves a spare pencil beside the plan.

arcEvents.title: What the Water Finds
lines: The repair materials arrive at the dock.
Lira tests each seam with shallow water.
One leaks immediately.
Lira: Good. Better here than beyond the headland.
You mark it and begin again.

arcEvents.title: The Old Tiller
lines: Corran takes the old tiller from his chest.
Corran: Your grandmother’s hand wore this smooth.
Lira: I can fit it without hiding the wear.
He asks to inspect the life belts.
She hands him the checklist.

arcEvents.title: A Name Before Launch
lines: The boat rests at the water’s edge.
Lira asks whether its first journey should follow the familiar coast or the cove route.
Both begin with a weather check.
Corran chooses his own place aboard.
Lira: We can turn back whenever we need.

arcEvents.title: Beyond the Headland
lines: The repaired hull holds a clean steady line.
Corran loosens his grip on the gunwale.
Lira: Deep water ahead. Ready when you are.
The coast opens into new fishing grounds.
On the return, nobody calls the trip small.

arcEvents.title: The Photograph
lines: A photograph slips from Halverd’s case.
It shows a bandstand beside a closed mine.
Halverd: Our town was promised a replacement industry. It never came.
He picks up the image before the proposal.
Halverd: I thought certainty was the kindest offer.

arcEvents.title: The Unmarked Path
lines: Halverd’s survey line crosses a footpath used by three families.
You walk it together.
At the far end, Rosalind waits with feed for a neighbor.
Halverd erases the line.
Halverd: The map omitted the reason the path exists.

arcEvents.title: A Different Report
lines: Halverd reads his draft by the inn fire.
It recommends local ownership and a longer debt schedule.
Halverd: My employer did not ask for this conclusion.
Marta: Is it the one you believe?
He puts his name beneath it.

arcEvents.title: The Resignation
lines: Halverd has written a resignation and a transfer request.
The first would let him start a small local surveying office.
The second would take him away with the revised report on record.
Halverd: I would value your view. The responsibility remains mine.
He waits without opening his sales case.

arcEvents.title: Lines That Serve
lines: Halverd hands Odalie a map showing paths, water access, and shared boundaries.
Halverd: No purchase proposal is attached.
If he stays, a modest office sign goes up beside the town hall.
If he leaves, his forwarding address remains on the notice board.
The valley keeps the right to name its own future.

marriageEvents.title: The Shared Shelf
lines: Ivy has filled the kitchen shelf with baking tins.
Then she notices your own things on the floor.
Ivy: I planned a kitchen and forgot we both live in it.
You rearrange the shelf together, leaving a space neither has claimed.
Ivy: There. Room for a recipe we haven’t found.

marriageEvents.title: A Burnt Breakfast
lines: A smoky pan waits on the stove.
Ivy: I wanted to make a perfect anniversary breakfast.
You open a window and find the bread that survived.
The two of you eat on the doorstep, laughing gently.
Ivy: I think I’ll remember this better than perfect.

marriageEvents.title: The Bakery’s Late Night
lines: Ivy has taken one order too many.
She starts to promise she can do it all.
Then she stops and asks you to help wrap the finished loaves.
Together you decide which future orders can wait.
The bakery closes with enough energy left for the walk home.

marriageEvents.title: The Family Recipe
lines: Ivy writes a new recipe into the household book.
There is room below it for a child’s future scribble or a visitor’s correction.
Ivy: Families can arrive in more than one way.
You talk about the life you want, without a deadline.
She closes the book only when both of you have finished speaking.

marriageEvents.title: Two Morning Rounds
lines: Kip has fed the animals before you wake.
You thank him, then show him the list of chores you hoped to share.
Kip: I thought doing everything would prove I belonged here.
You divide the morning so neither of you disappears into work.
There is time for breakfast together.

marriageEvents.title: A Guest at Supper
lines: Kip worries he will lose his words when guests arrive.
You agree on a little signal for when he needs a pause.
At supper, he tells a story about the first calf he named.
Everyone listens without rushing the ending.
Afterward he squeezes your hand beneath the table.

marriageEvents.title: The Quiet Anniversary
lines: Kip has set two mugs on the paddock bench.
Kip: I couldn’t think of anything grand enough.
The evening animals move through familiar grass.
You tell him what this ordinary place means to you.
The mugs stay warm between your hands.

marriageEvents.title: A Room for Someone Small
lines: Kip looks at the spare room and then at you.
Kip: If we ever welcome a child, I want them to know quiet doesn’t mean alone.
You discuss birth or adoption as choices deserving the same welcome.
There is no need to decide before either is ready.
He leaves the door open while you finish talking.

marriageEvents.title: The Coat Hook
lines: Ansel hangs the clinic coat inside the front door.
He reaches for a chart in its pocket, then pauses.
Ansel: I brought work home without asking the evening.
You agree where urgent work belongs and where supper begins.
The coat stays on its hook through dinner.

marriageEvents.title: Being the One Cared For
lines: Ansel wakes tired and immediately apologizes.
You set breakfast where he can reach it.
Ansel: I know what I would tell somebody else.
He smiles, eats, and takes the rest he needs.
The house does not require him to earn kindness.

marriageEvents.title: A Tune at Home
lines: Ansel hums while washing the cups.
He catches you listening and starts again from the beginning.
You keep time with the dish towel.
The kitchen fills with a song neither of you needs to perform well.
The last cup dries long after the music ends.

marriageEvents.title: A Family Conversation
lines: Ansel asks whether you would like to talk about children.
He carefully puts aside every assumption his profession has taught him to make.
You consider adoption or a birth announcement as equal paths to a wanted family.
Ansel: We choose together, and only when we’re ready.
The conversation ends with room for another day.

marriageEvents.title: The Rope by the Door
lines: A coil of rope occupies the space where your boots usually go.
Lira starts to defend its practical value, then laughs.
Lira: We need a house plan, not a maritime incident.
You add a sturdy hook beside the door.
Both the rope and the boots find a home.

marriageEvents.title: A Journey Apart
lines: Lira has an invitation to a two-day boat repair workshop.
She asks how it fits with the farm’s busy week.
You make a plan for chores, travel, and a letter on arrival.
Lira: I like having a home that doesn’t ask me to stop learning.
The return date goes on the kitchen calendar.

marriageEvents.title: Coming Back in Rain
lines: Lira arrives wet, tired, and quietly happy.
You set her boots by the door while she tells the least dramatic part first.
Lira: I thought about this kitchen every time the weather turned.
The kettle makes the windows mist.
The journey ends in two mugs and a comfortable chair.

marriageEvents.title: A Small Life Belt
lines: Lira has drawn a tiny life belt in the margin of a boat plan.
Lira: Perhaps someday. If we both want it.
You talk about welcoming a child through birth or adoption, and about making both farm and boat safe.
She adds a note to ask rather than assume.
The plan remains open between you.

marriageEvents.title: A Corner of One’s Own
lines: Sable has kept all their supplies packed in a traveling case.
Sable: I didn’t want to take over your home.
You choose a corner with good light together.
They unpack the brushes one at a time.
The empty case finally goes into storage.

marriageEvents.title: The Unflattering Sketch
lines: Sable shows you a sketch of both of you tired after chores.
There is dirt on your face and paint on their collar.
Sable: It feels more like us than the formal portrait.
You hang it where you will see it at breakfast.
Neither face needs improving to belong there.

marriageEvents.title: A Day without Making
lines: Sable leaves the sketchbook at home on purpose.
You walk until the village becomes small below you.
Sable: I don’t have to keep every good thing by turning it into work.
You share a quiet lunch and watch a cloud change.
The memory belongs to both of you without a signature.

marriageEvents.title: The Low Picture Rail
lines: Sable sketches a low picture rail for the spare room.
Sable: If we welcome a child, I want their view of the house to matter.
You talk about adoption or birth and the time a family needs.
They draw a little space for pictures nobody can predict.
The page remains a possibility, warmly held.

arcs.name: Marta and the Inn
arcs.epilogue: The inn’s welcome survives because its work and decisions are shared. Whether Marta leads a renovated inn or the village forms a co-op, a tired traveler still finds a lit doorway.

arcs.name: Dex: Leave or Stay
arcs.epilogue: Dex chooses a future with his own name on it. In the city he sends letters and returns each winter; at home he establishes a weekly music night. Neither choice closes the inn’s door.

arcs.name: Hollis and June
arcs.epilogue: Hollis and June share care of the bee farm without demanding identical lives. Pip’s family-honey sign hangs on the shed, and each sibling’s work is named in the new plan.

arcs.name: Dr. Ansel’s Burnout
arcs.epilogue: A substitute rota gives Ansel regular rest and the clinic reliable cover. He remains a careful doctor while recovering room for friendship, music, and a life beyond being needed.

arcs.name: Sable the Newcomer
arcs.epilogue: The town hall gallery holds portraits painted with each subject’s consent. Sable’s signature is easy to read, and a low wall leaves room for the children’s work.

arcs.name: Ivy’s Bakery
arcs.epilogue: Ivy opens the side-room bakery with a fair budget and her own name above the counter. Her parents support a business plan that includes her time, wages, and ambition.

arcs.name: Kip’s Confidence
arcs.epilogue: Kip leads the animal show with patient, clear instructions. His confidence grows from helping others feel safe, rather than becoming a different, louder person.

arcs.name: Lira’s Boat
arcs.epilogue: A repaired boat opens deep-water fishing and the hidden cove. Lira’s careful preparation lets Corran return to the water on his own terms.

arcs.name: Halverd’s Map
arcs.epilogue: Halverd faces the distance between protection and control. He can leave the consortium and open a local surveying office, or depart after changing his recommendation; either outcome respects the village’s right to decide.

chapters.title: The Stone in the Roots
chapters.objective: Clear the orchard with Iron tools, plant three fruit saplings, ship 50 spring crops, and reach three hearts with Bram.
lines: Bram rests a hand on the oldest stump.
Bram: Wren held the beam while I drove the first nail.
Bram: I called this workshop mine for years. It never was mine alone.
The cleared root gives way around a smooth green stone.
Bram: She thought the orchard would outlive both of us.
Bram: Planting it again is a fair answer.
At the square, one closed bud shines faintly.
Ilse: Something remembered how to begin.

chapters.title: The Stone Under the Falls
chapters.objective: Catch 15 fish species, repair Lira’s boat with wood and iron, and reach four hearts with Corran to sail to the cove.
lines: Corran checks the knot, then leaves it alone.
Corran: Wren pulled me aboard. I pulled her back when the next wave came.
Corran: I have made her the whole hero because it was easier than remembering my own hands.
Lira: Then today we all have hands. And life belts.
The boat passes through the falls’ cool curtain.
In the cove, a blue stone rests above the tide line.
Corran: We sheltered here until morning.
Lira: We can shelter here again without staying forever.
A second bud opens at the Lantern Tree.

chapters.title: The Stone in the Deep
chapters.objective: Reach mine floor 50, earn Greta’s trust, and bring Wren’s forge letter to her.
lines: The chamber wall carries two sets of initials: G.V. and W.
Greta holds the letter away from the forge’s heat.
Wren’s letter: I wanted you beside me on the road. I mistook your staying for refusing me.
Greta: I wanted her to ask what I loved here.
Greta: Neither of us was much good at the question that mattered.
An amber stone waits in their old quenching basin.
Greta: Take it. We made this room together.
Greta: And leave me some paper. I have an answer to write.
The third bud glows like metal cooling into strength.

chapters.title: The Stone in the Hearth
chapters.objective: Reach three hearts with ten villagers, advance three villager arcs to their midpoint, and gather for Longnight.
lines: Odalie puts down an unfinished list.
Odalie: I thought asking for help would mean I had failed you.
Marta: Then we have all failed into a very good supper.
Pip carries the spoons. Bram unfolds another bench.
Ivy tears the bread. Halverd adds a log without making a speech.
Ilse: The fourth hearthstone was never waiting in the ground.
Ilse: A hearth is a place people agree to keep warm.
A white ember rises above the fire and settles into your hands without burning.
Outside, the fourth bud holds its light against the snow.

journalPages.title: Under the Loose Board
journalPages.hint: The orchard’s oldest stump hides a green seam.
journalPages.text: I hid this page under the floor because a diary left on a desk begins to expect a tidy life. Mine has been neither tidy nor especially well planned. The farm looked smaller when I bought it. That was before I learned how far a bucket becomes when you carry it twice. Bram says the old orchard can be saved if I stop calling every bent tree a tragedy. He has offered to help after his workshop roof is finished. I shall help with the roof first. Perhaps that is how a place becomes home: one job discovering that it belongs beside another.

journalPages.title: A Workshop with Two Names
journalPages.hint: Bram’s three saplings mark a new beginning.
journalPages.text: We raised the last workshop beam today. Bram measured it so often I began to think the wood might feel accused. I held the far end, sang badly, and pretended the weight was easier than it was. Afterward we planted three orchard saplings with the dirt still under our nails. He said a building was a promise to stay useful. I said a tree was a promise to wait. Neither of us knew what to say about leaving. There was a green stone caught in the oldest root. We left it there, sheltered by work that had already begun before either of us arrived.

journalPages.title: The Margin of the Record
journalPages.hint: Ask Fenwick about the four lights, not four rocks.
journalPages.text: The archive lists four hearthstones but never describes their weight. Fenwick found that frustrating. I found it promising. One page calls them gifts, another calls them duties, and a third was used to settle an argument about a borrowed cart. Histories are wonderfully untidy when nobody has polished them for visitors. In the margin, someone drew four little lights around a table. I copied the drawing and forgot the official date. If you come after me looking for treasure, read the margins too. People put what matters there when the important part of the page has already been claimed by someone important.

journalPages.title: What Corran Pulled Ashore
journalPages.hint: A repaired tiller can carry an old memory safely.
journalPages.text: Corran remembers the rope in my hands. I remember his coat beneath my fingers when the boat pitched and I nearly followed the water. Neither memory is complete alone. We reached the little cove behind the falls and sat with our backs against the stone until dawn. Nobody said anything brave. We asked whether the others were warm enough, then asked again because there was nothing else we could change. I want that part written down. Rescue is not always a shining moment. Sometimes it is cold people refusing to let one another become more cold, one ordinary question at a time.

journalPages.title: The Dry Ledge
journalPages.hint: The blue Hearthstone rests above the highest tide mark.
journalPages.text: There is a ledge in the cove that stays dry when the tide rises. I have marked it with three scratches, not because it belongs to me, but because somebody frightened might need to see them quickly. We left a blue stone there. Corran said it had been warming his pocket all night, though neither of us could explain how. I do not think every useful thing needs an explanation before it can be shared. We also left a wrapped candle and a little dry kindling. Replace those if you use them. A marvel is welcome, but a second chance to light a fire is practical kindness.

journalPages.title: An Unfinished Descent
journalPages.hint: Carry food and keep the route back clear.
journalPages.text: Greta says I walk into the mine as if curiosity will hold up the ceiling. Today she made me carry the lantern and name every turn before we went farther. I was irritated until I had to find the way back while tired. Then I was grateful, which is less comfortable when someone has already warned you. We stopped before reaching the chamber we wanted. I called that failure. Greta called it supper. Supper was excellent. I write this for whichever future version of me forgets: there is no prize for arriving at a beautiful place too exhausted to leave it safely.

journalPages.title: The Sound of Two Hammers
journalPages.hint: The old forge chamber lies ten floors below.
journalPages.text: You can hear a second hammer down here when two people work in rhythm. The sound arrives a little late from the far wall, as though the mountain wants a turn. Greta showed me how to hold a piece steady without fighting every movement. I thought friendship worked like that too, but I never said it. I was younger and inclined to save my best sentences for paper. On the wall near the lower passage we scratched our initials. Mine is deeper because I wanted it noticed. Hers is straighter because she wanted it right. The mountain has room for both mistakes.

journalPages.title: A Pocket of Night
journalPages.hint: Starglass is a fitting material for a promise.
journalPages.text: At the deepest ledge the light catches tiny clear fragments in the rock. Greta calls them Starglass because she refuses to name a beautiful thing merely by what it costs. I kept one in a cloth and looked at it that night beside the farmhouse window. It was less impressive than it had been underground. That did not make it false. Some things shine because of where you meet them, or who is standing beside you. If you use such a fragment in a ring, remember that a promise will have ordinary mornings as well as luminous ones. Make it strong enough for both.

journalPages.title: A Letter I Should Have Sent
journalPages.hint: Give Greta the words before asking for an answer.
journalPages.text: Greta, I thought you would travel because I wanted you beside me. When you chose the forge, I heard that you did not choose me. It was a selfish translation. You had a shop, people who trusted your work, and a future you could see through your own doorway. I should have asked about that future before filling it with mine. I still wish we had shared some roads. I also wish I had made it easier for you to welcome me home. This page may reach you late. It carries no excuse for the delay, only the words I should have trusted you with sooner.

journalPages.title: The Path Beneath the Candles
journalPages.hint: Follow the low lights where the forest path bends.
journalPages.text: Ilse moved the Ember Walk path around a growing root this year. Someone objected that the old route was traditional. She asked whether tripping over the root was traditional too. I laughed before I could pretend to be solemn. Later she told me the walk was not meant to preserve every footstep. It was meant to help people arrive together carrying a little light. I have been thinking about the arguments we call loyalty. Sometimes we protect a path so fiercely that we forget the people using it. Next year I will bring a spare candle, and perhaps a little less certainty.

journalPages.title: Who Brought the Wood
journalPages.hint: The final Hearthstone begins with ten friendships and shared work.
journalPages.text: The feast nearly failed because everyone assumed someone else had arranged the wood. Then everyone assumed Ilse would know whose fault it was. She handed me an empty basket. We carried logs from four houses, each with a different smell, and the room warmed before the argument finished. I watched people move their chairs closer without being asked. A hearth is stone around a fire, yes, but that definition leaves out the person who notices an empty woodbox. If the old story speaks of a winter hearthstone, perhaps it means the moment we stop asking whose job warmth is and begin carrying it.

journalPages.title: The Merchant’s Recipe Box
journalPages.hint: A good preserving recipe leaves room for the actual fruit.
journalPages.text: Ozzie sold me a recipe box with no recipes in it. He called it an opportunity for culinary independence. I called it a box and paid accordingly. I have filled it slowly with meals people taught me while I was supposed to be doing something else. Marta measures soup by who is coming. Noor measures rice with a finger against the pot. Greta measures tea by whether the cup is visible through it. The recipes are not exact, but their generosity is. When you cook from them, begin with what you have, taste what you made, and leave enough for an unexpected chair.

journalPages.title: A Road with No Appointment
journalPages.hint: Travel has not changed the farm’s welcome.
journalPages.text: This morning I reached a village whose name I had never needed to know. Nobody expected me there. For an hour that felt like freedom, and then it felt like being very small. A woman at a stall asked whether I had eaten. I said yes because I did not want to be troublesome. She handed me a pear anyway. I thought of Rosalind and nearly turned for home. Instead I sat on a wall and ate the pear properly. I am trying to learn that leaving need not mean refusing every reminder of what I love. Please eat before your work begins tomorrow.

journalPages.title: The Unsent Postcard
journalPages.hint: There are sixteen pages; twelve can show Wren the way home for the vote.
journalPages.text: I bought a postcard for Greta in a mountain town where the forge was painted blue. For three days I carried it without writing. Every cheerful sentence sounded like a claim that I had been right to leave, and every sad one sounded like asking her to admit I had been wrong. Today I wrote about the hinge on the inn door. She would have hated it. That gave me a true beginning. I have tucked this page beside the postcard because I want you to know how small a first step can be. A difficult letter need not begin with the difficult part. It must simply begin honestly.

journalPages.title: A Keeper’s Empty Hands
journalPages.hint: Care for the tree after its light returns.
journalPages.text: I asked Ilse what she guarded in the chapel. She opened both hands and said that guarding was not quite her work. She tended things people needed to be able to approach. The difference stayed with me. I have guarded my independence so carefully that sometimes my friends must knock twice before I let them help. Perhaps the farm has suffered the same habit in me. If you inherit it, please do not preserve every decision I made. Move the gate if another path is kinder. Put a table where I kept a trunk. A home worth passing on must remain possible to enter.

journalPages.title: Dawn Without an Audience
journalPages.hint: The summit offers its winter light before the village wakes.
journalPages.text: I reached the summit before dawn and expected a revelation worthy of the climb. Mostly I was cold. Then the first light touched the roofs below, one at a time, and I knew whose kitchen lay under each patch of snow. The valley looked less like a beautiful view than a collection of people beginning difficult, ordinary mornings. I could not see my own farmhouse until the sun moved farther. It belonged to the picture without needing to stand at the center. I think I will travel. I think I will return. Neither decision cancels the work of loving this place while I am here.

letters.title: A Letter from the Road
letters.text: Dear one, I reached a village with blue shutters and an excellent pear stall. I thought of our kitchen while eating breakfast on a wall. The road is good to me, but I want to know how the first planting went. You may tell me about the failures too. I left a page beneath the loose farmhouse board, near the bed. Keep what helps and argue with the rest. Love, Wren.

letters.title: A Map with Watermarks
letters.text: Dear one, I have enclosed a little map Corran once drew on the back of a packing list. It shows the coast more accurately than its scale suggests. Ask him about the cove, but let him decide how much of the story to tell. A boat can carry old grief without making it the captain. Please take water when you work in the heat. I know how you forget. With love, Wren.

letters.title: The Postcard I Finally Sent
letters.text: Dear one, I have finally written to Greta. For years I imagined an apology needed to be grand enough to justify the delay. It needed to arrive. If you find my forge page, please give her the words without asking her to forgive on a schedule. I have seen marvelous mountains. None has made a familiar kitchen less valuable. Send me one ordinary thing about your week. Love, Wren.

letters.title: A Place at the Table
letters.text: Dear one, winter has brought me to a house where everyone brings a dish and nobody knows whose spoon is whose. I am thinking of Longnight. Do not let Odalie carry the whole gathering on that formidable clipboard. Bring people into the work early, and leave room at the table for someone you did not expect. I miss you. That sentence does not need an adventurous ending. Love, Wren.

letters.title: Three Saplings
letters.text: The old nursery still answers my letters. Three fruit saplings should reach the shop in time for your orchard work. Clear the old stumps with Iron tools first; don’t plant around a problem you can solve properly. I can meet you there once we know each other a little better. Bring a spade. I’ll bring the stakes. Bram.

letters.title: Your Tool Is Ready
letters.text: The repair is finished. Pick it up when the forge is open, and keep the edge clean this time. I’ve fitted the grip to your hand rather than the catalog drawing. Don’t thank me in a speech. Use it well. Greta.

letters.title: Boat Repair List
letters.text: I need sound wood, iron fittings, and somebody willing to hold the other end while I measure. We test the hull before launching, not afterward while shouting. Granddad has the old tiller. Ask gently if he’s ready to show it. There’s deep water beyond the headland when we finish. I’ve saved you the least splashy seat. Lira.

letters.title: The Basket Came Back Full
letters.text: I sent your basket home with supper inside. That is not repayment; that is how baskets ought to travel. The ingredients helped, but knowing somebody had noticed helped more. Come by when you are hungry or when you need a room with people in it. The stove will be on. Marta.

letters.title: First Morning Invitation
letters.text: The bakery counter is ready. I have counted the trays six times and slept approximately none. Please come when you can, and tell me honestly what you think. The little table by the window is real now. Dad keeps polishing it. Mum says that is his way of making a speech. Bring an appetite. Ivy.

letters.title: Clinic Hours and Cover
letters.text: The new clinic rota is posted by the door. A neighboring doctor will cover my regular afternoon off; urgent-care instructions and contact details are displayed there too. Rest will not mean leaving anyone without care. Thank you for helping me understand the difference between dedication and exhaustion. I hope to see you sometimes simply as a friend. Ansel.

letters.title: An Invitation with My Name
letters.text: The town hall gallery opens this week. Everyone pictured has seen and approved their portrait, though Greta said approval sounded too enthusiastic. Children’s work hangs low enough for children to see it. My name is on the poster, clearly this time. You helped me believe I could put it there. I would like you beside me when the doors open. Sable.

letters.title: A Room Above the Music Hall
letters.text: I found the room. The ceiling is low, the street is loud, and the piano downstairs has different wrong notes from ours. I miss the inn without wishing I had never left. Please tell Mum I made soup, with actual vegetables. I will come home each winter, and sooner if the timetable permits. Thank you for making my choice feel like mine. Dex.

letters.title: Friday Music at the Inn
letters.text: We are moving the small tables after supper and putting chairs where the audience can see. I want a proper music night, with local songs, visitors, and room for beginners. Staying has begun to feel like building something rather than forgetting to leave. Come early if you want the seat beside the stove. I saved a new tune for the opening. Dex.

letters.title: The Family Plan
letters.text: Hollis and I have written a farm plan that names both our work and the time we need elsewhere. It is not a perfect agreement, but it is one we can review together. Pip decorated the top with three enormous bees. Thank you for helping us speak without deciding one of us had to be the villain. The next jar of honey is for you. June.

letters.title: A Revised Recommendation
letters.text: Please find notice that my recommendation to the consortium has changed. I have documented the valley’s active farms, shared services, and viable local plans, and requested a pause on acquisition. This does not oblige you to trust me, nor does it replace the council’s right to decide. I appreciate the evidence you offered and the questions I should have asked sooner. Cyprian Halverd.

letters.title: A Ribbon Worth Asking About
letters.text: I have added Willow Ribbons to the cart. Their purpose is straightforward even if the conversation feels less so: when you know someone well, a ribbon can ask whether they would like to share more of your days. No grand performance required. I also stock ordinary twine for conversations with fenceposts. Your devoted traveling supplier, Ozzie.

letters.title: A Small Reminder
letters.text: The birthday calendar is on the town board. Please remember that a visit can be as welcome as a parcel, and that nobody is required to organize a committee. This last point applies particularly to the mayor. We are glad you are part of the village’s year now. Odalie.

letters.title: Keep Tending the Light
letters.text: The tree has bloomed. Tomorrow it will still need water, clear ground, and people willing to notice a broken branch. We will gather each Spring 1 for the Lantern Bloom Vigil. It is a celebration of the light and a reminder of the ordinary work that welcomed it back. Bring breakfast if you like. Pip has made a persuasive case. Ilse.

letters.title: The Road Home
letters.text: Dear one, your pages have found me in a dozen borrowed rooms. Taken together, they tell a story I had left scattered. I am coming home for the vote. I will not arrive with an answer the village must accept, but with my own chair to carry and my own voice to offer. Keep the kettle where you like it. I can learn a changed kitchen. All my love, Wren.

letters.title: I Kept the Speech
letters.text: The show went well. Rosalind says I know that and do not need her to confirm it, which she confirmed twice. I kept the speech, but I did not need to look at the last page. Thank you for practicing with me without pretending I was already fearless. I am glad the animals had a calm day too. Kip.

tv.title: Reading the Sky
tv.text: Clouds are a forecast, not a promise. Check tomorrow’s report before planning a long mine trip.

tv.title: A Rainy Morning
tv.text: Rain waters outdoor fields. Use the saved watering time for repairs, visits, or a careful rest.

tv.title: Heat on the Hills
tv.text: On hot days, work in smaller stretches and carry food and water. Your field can wait while you recover.

tv.title: Snow at the Threshold
tv.text: Snow does not replace liquid water for a thirsty plant under glass. Check the greenhouse by hand.

tv.title: Storm Preparations
tv.text: Bring livestock indoors before severe weather and check the feed supply. A latch is cheaper than a worried night.

tv.title: Wind and Leaves
tv.text: Autumn wind gathers leaves against gates. Clear the entrance before assuming the hinge has failed.

tv.title: A Clear Winter Dawn
tv.text: For those visiting the summit, dawn arrives before the village wakes. Dress warmly and plan the return.

tv.title: The Day After Tomorrow
tv.text: The longer-range forecast is less certain. Keep one part of your workday flexible.

tv.title: River After Rain
tv.text: Fast runoff can change a familiar fishing spot. Watch the current before choosing where to stand.

tv.title: A Dry Afternoon
tv.text: Dry air helps stored hay and repaired wood. It does not make an exhausted farmer more durable.

tv.title: Frost and Timing
tv.text: Late planting deserves a look at the calendar. A crop cannot negotiate with the next season.

tv.title: A Cloudy Day
tv.text: Soft light can make an ordinary walk beautiful. The forecast offers no objection to enjoying it.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Gentle Heat
tv.text: A simmer makes small regular bubbles. If the pot is leaping, lower the heat before the bottom catches.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Taste First
tv.text: Taste fruit before adding sugar. The harvest has already done part of the recipe.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Bread Rest
tv.text: Dough needs time as well as effort. Resting it can make the next knead easier than extra force.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Soup Shares
tv.text: When another guest arrives, add cooked beans and a little water, then taste again. Generosity still needs seasoning.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Clean Boards
tv.text: Use a clean board and wash your hands between ingredients. A meal should leave only good memories.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: The Warm Plate
tv.text: Warm a serving plate gently before setting out winter supper. Small comforts travel through ordinary dishes.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: A Sharp Knife
tv.text: A sharp kitchen knife needs less force. Keep fingers curled and work on a steady board.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Leftover Rice
tv.text: Cool leftovers promptly and store them safely. Tomorrow’s lunch begins with today’s careful kitchen.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Herb Stems
tv.text: Tender herb stems can flavor a simmering pot. Tie them together if you want to remove them easily.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Roasted Roots
tv.text: Cut root vegetables to similar sizes so the smallest piece does not finish before its neighbors.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: A Little Salt
tv.text: If a dish tastes dull, test a spoonful with a small pinch of salt before changing the whole pot.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: An Honest Failure
tv.text: Write down what went wrong while you remember it. A recipe notebook is allowed to contain mistakes.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Shared Bread
tv.text: For a feast, bake a loaf people can tear into portions. The shape can make sharing feel natural.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Gentle Eggs
tv.text: Take eggs off the heat just before they look entirely finished. The warm pan keeps working.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Clean Jars
tv.text: Preserving calls for clean equipment and a tested process. A pretty jar is not the same as a safe seal.

tv.title: Willowmere Kitchen: Cooking Together
tv.text: Before a shared recipe, decide who cuts, who stirs, and who reads. Fewer elbows make a calmer meal.

tv.title: Workshop Notice
tv.text: Bram is collecting repair requests before winter. Bring measurements if you have them and the broken piece if you can.

tv.title: A Fair Counter
tv.text: The general store welcomes small orders. Starting with one seed packet is still starting.

tv.title: The Reading Chair
tv.text: The library has moved a chair beside the low shelves so young readers can choose books comfortably.

tv.title: Animal Show Invitation
tv.text: Kip reminds first-time handlers that animals get time to settle before judging begins.

tv.title: A Table at the Inn
tv.text: Marta invites neighbors to sit by the fire even when they are not ordering supper.

tv.title: Gallery Courtesy
tv.text: Ask before touching or photographing a portrait. The person pictured helped choose how they are shown.

tv.title: Clinic Rota
tv.text: Check the clinic door for cover arrangements. A rested doctor and reliable care belong in the same plan.

tv.title: Seedling Cart
tv.text: Festival volunteers welcome spare flowers, careful hands, and anyone willing to sweep afterward.

tv.title: Market Road
tv.text: Ozzie’s cart visits on market days. Curiosity is welcome even when your purse is staying closed.

tv.title: The Council Door
tv.text: Questions for the council may be written or spoken. Odalie asks that quieter voices get their turn.

tv.title: A Clear Path
tv.text: Neighbors are asked to keep shared paths passable. The person who needs them may be carrying something heavy.

tv.title: Honey Labels
tv.text: The Marrow honey stall is labeling jars by harvest and flower source. A familiar jar may hold a different season.

tv.title: Library Returns
tv.text: A late book is welcome back. Fenwick promises to greet the book before discussing the date.

tv.title: Music After Supper
tv.text: The inn piano is available by arrangement. Listeners count as participants.

tv.title: A Living Orchard
tv.text: New saplings need support, water, and space for their roots. A planted tree begins a continuing job.

tv.title: Longnight Contributions
tv.text: Please tell the inn what you are bringing for Longnight. The village appreciates dishes as well as chairs.

tv.title: The Borrowed Lantern
tv.text: A traveler borrowed a lantern and returned it with fresh oil. By winter, nobody remembered its first owner, but every house knew where to find a light.

tv.title: The Honest Bridge
tv.text: A carpenter built a bridge too narrow for carts. Rather than call it a miracle of economy, she wrote a sign asking for help to widen it.

tv.title: The Four Cups
tv.text: Four neighbors argued over the best spring water. When they poured their samples into the soup pot, supper improved and the argument became less urgent.

tv.title: The Listening Stone
tv.text: A child told worries to a stone by the river. An elder sat nearby and learned that the stone’s best feature was its patience.

tv.title: The Wind’s Coat
tv.text: A tailor promised to sew the wind a coat. After chasing it for a week, he made warm coats for the people standing in it instead.

tv.title: The Empty Basket
tv.text: A farmer carried an empty basket to the feast, ashamed of a failed harvest. The village filled it with leftovers and asked for help washing the bowls.

tv.title: The Returning Path
tv.text: Two siblings took different paths around a hill. When they met again, each had found a flower the other had never seen.

tv.title: The Candle Keeper
tv.text: A keeper lit one candle before the visitors came. When asked whether anyone would arrive, she said the light was how they would know they could.

tv.title: The Crooked Spoon
tv.text: A wooden spoon bent with age. Its owner kept it because it reached the corner of the pot better than when it was new.

tv.title: The Unfinished Map
tv.text: A mapmaker left room at every edge. People complained until a child drew the path to a newly built house.

tv.title: The Snow Bench
tv.text: Villagers cleared one bench after every snowfall. Nobody could recall who began it, but nobody had to stand alone through a difficult conversation.

tv.title: The Quiet Bell
tv.text: A chapel bell cracked and sounded softer. The village kept it because people began listening for one another instead of waiting to be called.

tv.title: The Second Loaf
tv.text: A baker made a second loaf for an expected guest. When the guest did not come, the baker discovered how many neighbors had skipped supper.

tv.title: The Well Rope
tv.text: A well rope broke where many hands had worn it smooth. The new rope was bought by everyone who had ever carried a bucket home.

tv.title: The Patient Gate
tv.text: A gate stuck every spring. One year a child noticed the tree root beneath it. The gate moved; the tree stayed; everyone reached the garden.

tv.title: The Last Ember
tv.text: During a long winter night, each house brought one ember to the meeting hall. Nobody could identify their own flame once the room was warm.

intro: The city office has gone dark except for one desk.
A letter lies beside work that will still be waiting tomorrow.
Dear one, I have left the farm to you, and left myself a little road to follow.
You need not become the person I was. The valley has room for somebody I have not imagined yet.
There is a kettle on the stove, a stubborn gate, and more weeds than any reasonable farewell should contain.
Look after the valley and the tree. Ask for help. I failed at that last part more often than I admitted.
The farm is a gift, not a debt. Make a life you can bear to wake up inside.
With all my love, Aunt Wren.
The cart reaches Willowmere as the square begins its morning.
Odalie: Welcome. I had a speech, but the cart is early and you look tired.
Odalie: Your aunt’s farm needs work. There is also a council vote coming, about an offer from a consortium.
Odalie: I wish I could give you only the first piece of news.
Rosalind: You can give the farmer breakfast before either piece grows teeth.
At the farm, a patch of clear earth waits beside the weeds.
Odalie: Start here. Clear one patch, till it, plant a turnip, and water it.
Rosalind: The shipping box takes what you can spare. The bed takes you before you fall over.
Odalie: The rest can begin tomorrow.

endings.title: Thriving Willowmere
lines: The last hand rises. The vote is unanimous.
Odalie: The land remains with the village. The work remains with all of us.
The council offers you a chair, with your name written on a card instead of a title carved in stone.
Ivy opens the bakery shutters. Dex’s music travels through the inn.
Kip calls the next animal into the show without checking his sleeve.
A map in Halverd’s new office marks footpaths as carefully as property lines.
Under the Lantern Tree, Wren reaches for another empty cup.
Wren: There you are. Tell me what you’re planting next.
Morning comes to a farm with work still waiting, and a village willing to share it.

endings.title: Steady Willowmere
lines: The vote passes by a narrow margin.
Odalie lets out a breath she has been holding since the first speech.
Odalie: A promise is not a finished bridge. We begin building tomorrow.
Some repairs remain on the notice board. Some conversations need another evening.
The Lantern Tree keeps its light while villagers put the chairs away.
Marta sends supper home with whoever stayed to sweep.
Bram: Narrow is wide enough for the first step.
Your farm waits beyond the square, still growing into the life you have made.
There will be another season to tend together.

endings.title: Uncertain Willowmere
lines: The proposal fails to secure enough support for keeping the land as it is.
Nobody cheers. Nobody is asked to leave.
Odalie: The sale is delayed for one year. We owe this village time to answer properly.
Halverd closes his case without taking out a contract.
Ilse: An unlit branch is still alive.
The chapter goals remain in your journal. The people remain at their doors.
Bring the four Hearthstones together, and the council will meet again.
The morning after the vote is an ordinary farming morning.
Ordinary mornings are places where a different ending can begin.

bloom.title: Lantern Bloom
lines: Morning reaches the square before anyone remembers to ring the bell.
Four lights rise through the roots of the Lantern Tree.
The closed flowers open, one after another, until every branch holds a warm glow.
Bram: Look at that joint between the old branch and the new.
Greta: For once, leave the craftsmanship alone and look.
Corran reaches for Lira’s hand. Neither speaks.
Odalie: We will keep this morning. Every year, if we can.
Ilse: A vigil, then. Not for waiting on a miracle, but for remembering the work.
Pip: Can we have breakfast under it?
Marta: That is the first sensible motion of the day.
The square fills with borrowed chairs.
The Lantern Bloom Vigil is now part of Willowmere’s calendar.

vote.title: The Council Vote
lines: Odalie opens the town hall doors before placing her notes on the desk.
Odalie: Today we decide what sort of future we are willing to work for.
Bram: I have repaired houses here that still have good years in them.
Greta: So do the people inside them.
Pell: A shop survives because people come back.
Noor: And because their work is paid fairly.
Ivy: I want a future with space to begin something.
Rosalind: We have kept living things well. That ought to count.
Kip: I think everyone should get a turn to speak.
Ansel: We can care for each other without asking one person to do everything.
Marta: The inn has enough keys for a shared future.
Dex: Staying and leaving should both be choices, not punishments.
Corran: Fear is useful aboard a boat. It should not be the captain.
Lira: Give us plans we can repair with our own hands.
Sable: I came as a visitor. You let me put my name on the wall.
Fenwick: Let the record include the people who are not usually recorded.
Hollis: Work done quietly is still work.
June: So is learning to share it.
Ilse: The light is not our argument. The care that brought it back is.
Pip: Please keep the places where people sit together.
Ozzie: A road is worth traveling because of the places it connects.
Halverd: You are entitled to question every claim in my report, including my own.
Odalie: Then let us vote with open eyes, and keep the doors open afterward.

ivy: Ivy holds the Hearth Ring beside the flour mark on her hand.
Ivy: I want all our ordinary mornings, even the burnt ones.
She laughs before the tears have time to choose a direction.
Ivy: Yes. Let’s make a life we can keep changing together.
kip: Kip looks at the Hearth Ring, then at you.
Kip: I practiced what I might say if this ever happened.
He folds both hands gently around yours.
Kip: I don’t need the speech. Yes. I want to come home with you.
ansel: Ansel takes a steady breath before touching the ring.
Ansel: I want to be your partner, in work and in rest.
His smile is easier than the careful words.
Ansel: Yes. There is a whole life I would like to share with you.
lira: Lira turns the Hearth Ring toward the light.
Lira: A good promise needs room for journeys and a place to return.
She takes your hand with the same steady care she gives a mooring line.
Lira: Yes. Let’s keep choosing the way together.
sable: Sable studies the ring, then puts the little box aside.
Sable: I want to look at you while I answer.
Their hands tremble just enough for you to notice.
Sable: Yes. I would like to be in the picture with you, every day.

ivy: The Chapel of Seasons opens onto a square full of neighbors.
Ilse: A promise is not a prediction that life will be easy.
Ilse: It is an agreement to meet the life that comes with honest hands.
The Hearth Rings catch the light from the open door.
Ivy: I promise to make room for your hopes beside mine, and to ask for help before the kitchen fills with smoke.
You place the rings with hands steadied by one another.
Ilse: Then this village witnesses your choice and offers its help.
The chapel bell rings. Outside, borrowed tables wait beneath the tree.
Odalie: May your home make room for both your voices.
Bram: May the door open easily after a long day.
Greta: May your promises hold, and may you repair them when they need care.
Pell: May the cupboards be useful and the conversations plentiful.
Noor: May the work be shared fairly and the kindness given freely.
Rosalind: May you keep learning how the other needs to be loved.
Kip: May silence feel safe between you.
Ansel: May rest belong to the life you build.
Marta: May there always be another place at your table.
Dex: May your song have room for both melodies.
Corran: May you speak before the weather turns.
Lira: May every journey leave a way home.
Sable: May you keep looking closely at the person beside you.
Fenwick: May the everyday pages be worth remembering.
Hollis: May you notice work done quietly.
June: May you allow each other to grow without growing apart.
Ilse: May this promise be a hearth you both tend.
Pip: May you know where the spare cups are.
Ozzie: May surprises find you with dry socks and good company.
Halverd: May you measure success by a life you both chose.
Wren: May your home welcome the people you become.
The feast lasts until the lanterns are lit.
When you return to the farm, the doorway belongs to both of you.
