supplemental.text: I left the heel of the loaf for you. You said it was your favorite, and I remembered.
Our kitchen smells like toasted oats. I think that is a respectable beginning for a day.
You can tell me a batch failed. I married you because you are honest, not because you praise every biscuit.
The dough needs another hour. We could walk to the gate and forget to hurry back.
I drew a little wheat stalk beside our names in my recipe book.
I want a bakery window someday. I also want evenings here. I am working on a plan that allows both.
Your sleeves have flour on them again. I suspect my hugs are leaving evidence.
Please taste this filling before I sweeten it. Your thoughtful chewing face is very useful.
There is room beside my mixing bowl for your breakfast plate.
I woke up thinking about rye bread and then remembered you were here. An excellent pair of thoughts.
If I seem cross, ask whether I have eaten. Then ask what actually upset me.
We do not need an impressive dinner. Toast together sounds wonderful.
I practiced a new braid on the dough. Yours is the loaf with the lopsided end.
Noor taught me to wrap bread while it is just warm. I want our kitchen to have little teachings like that.
Pell asked whether we needed more jars. I said three. Expect a discussion about twelve.
I nearly signed a note with my old address. Then I smiled so much I spilled the ink.
Let us put a hook by the door for your hat. I keep rescuing it from the bread basket.
You look tired. Give me the watering can for a moment and tell me which row comes next.
I have ambitions that frighten me a little. Being able to say them at this table helps.
We should keep one shelf for experiments. Clearly labeled experiments, after the salt biscuit incident.
I made a very small cake because an ordinary evening deserves some icing too.
The oven clicked while I was reading. I know this house by its sounds now.
I love hearing your boots outside. Even when those boots bring half the field with them.
Would you hold the bowl? This batter is determined to redecorate the wall.
I saved that recipe you scribbled on the back of a seed packet. The dirt seems appropriate.
A bakery needs reliable opening hours. A marriage needs me to stop thinking about opening hours at dinner.
If we disagree about the curtains, we can look at more curtains. There is no prize for deciding tonight.
I bought cinnamon with my own savings. It feels good to bring a little luxury home.
I want you to have time for your friends. Tell them I will only interrogate them about bread briefly.
There is a dent in this tin from our first meal here. I have become absurdly fond of it.
You do not have to earn a quiet morning with me.
I tried shaping a bun like your favorite animal. It currently resembles a determined potato.
My apron pocket contains a ribbon from our wedding. Also crumbs. It is a very honest pocket.
Can we eat outside tonight? I want the bread to cool in the same breeze that moves the orchard.
I wrote down how you take your tea. I know it now, but I like seeing it there.
When I am rushing, remind me that the yeast does not care about my schedule.
We should invite my parents for supper soon. I will tell Pell that bringing a receipt is optional.
I am proud of the work you do when nobody comes by to admire it.
The sink is full, the bread is rising, and I am happy. These things can apparently happen together.
I want to hear the whole story about your day, including the part you think is boring.
I borrowed a cookbook from Fenwick. We must protect it from my enthusiasm and your jam spoon.
That first tray burned because I was watching you come up the path. I will accept half the blame.
I am learning to ask for help before the bowl falls off the counter.
Keep that crooked carrot for supper. It will fit perfectly once I chop it.
Let us choose something neither of us has cooked before. A shared disaster still counts as dinner practice.
I like how you leave room for me to change my mind.
I moved the good plates lower. Celebrations are easier when nobody needs a ladder.
There is a little honey on your cup. I was trying to make your morning sweeter with considerable precision.
I can work at my baking and love our home. Please remind me of that when I try to do everything at once.
The dough stuck to my ring today. I took it off to clean it and missed its weight immediately.
Would you read aloud while I knead? I promise my interruptions will mostly concern the story.
We have enough scraps for a bread pudding. I enjoy a second chance you can eat.
I want to learn the meal you missed most before you came here.
The first biscuit is still too hot. This is a warning to both of us.
Your side of the table catches the morning light. I find reasons to look that way.
I had a hard day. Could you sit with me before we work out how to fix it?
I set aside an afternoon with no orders. I would like to spend some of it holding your hand.
Our pantry labels have two kinds of handwriting now. That makes me happier than matching jars would.
I have a plan for tomorrow, but tonight I just want to hear you laugh.
Whatever the next loaf looks like, I am glad this is the kitchen I get to bring it into.
I heard you moving about and put another cup on the table. Still makes me smile.
The animals know your step now. They lift their heads before you reach the fence.
I patched the glove with the loose thumb. Try it before you go; I might have made the thumb ambitious.
Rosalind sent advice with the supper basket. The advice would not fit in the basket.
I like chores beside you. We can be quiet without the quiet feeling empty.
Your coat was damp, so I hung it near the warm spot. Not too close.
I used to practice what to say to you. Sometimes I still do, even over breakfast.
Could we sit by the pasture after supper? The sheep make very undemanding company.
I am glad you tell me when you need a hand. Guessing was never my strongest skill.
The little animals sleep with their feet tucked in. You do something similar with the blanket.
I brought home a smooth piece of wood for the gate latch. It should be easier on your hands.
You can leave the heavy bucket. I have time, and carrying it together is awkward but possible.
I think our house smells like tea and clean wool. That is a good smell to come home to.
There is no hurry to answer. I asked because I want to understand, not because I need a quick yes.
I worried I would be too quiet to share a home. You gave me room to find the words.
I saved you the chair that does not wobble. Bram can look at the other one when he visits.
The brush handle is wearing smooth where you hold it. Things tell you who cares for them.
I would like to visit the ranch today. Coming home afterward is something I look forward to too.
You have a way of making a long task feel possible. Even sorting the twine drawer.
I left a small knot in the fence rope to mark the weak post. We can check it together.
There is a feather on your shoulder. Hold still. There, now you look slightly less like a chicken.
Some days I miss a cue with people. You can tell me plainly if I missed one with you.
I want us to rest before we become too tired to be kind.
You remember the shy calf at the ranch? She let me rub her forehead. I wanted you to be the first to know.
I put the kettle on, then forgot to light the stove. It has been a thoughtful sort of morning.
That ribbon from the wedding is in my coat pocket. I touch it when a day feels crowded.
I am learning your favorite walks. There are more stops to look at things than I expected. I like that.
If you want company while you mend something, I can be the person who holds the thread.
I did not know I could miss someone between breakfast and lunch.
Rosalind says we need a bigger soup pot. I think she means she plans to visit often.
The barn sounds different when everyone settles. I would like to show you, if you have a quiet evening.
I had trouble saying what bothered me yesterday. I have the words now, if you have a moment.
I folded the blanket, mostly. One corner refuses to cooperate.
I like your laugh when you forget anyone is listening.
You need not finish every fence today. The last post will still be there tomorrow.
I checked the latch twice because I was thinking about our dinner plans. Both checks were reassuring.
Would you like me to bring something from the ranch? Apart from another story about a goat.
I put a bench cushion by the door. Sitting down to take off muddy boots is a fine invention.
I once thought a home had to be perfectly settled. Ours has projects in every corner, and I feel settled anyway.
I can tell when you are trying to be brave. You are allowed to lean on me too.
There is a soft patch of grass beyond the gate. I have been saving that discovery for us.
Your hands are cold. Mine are warm from carrying the tea, so this seems easily solved.
I am proud to introduce you as my spouse. Still stumble over the word sometimes. That is happiness.
We could make supper slowly. I am very qualified to peel one potato at a time.
I made room for your boots beside mine. The mud can negotiate its own arrangement.
When you ask about an animal, I sometimes answer for ten minutes. Thank you for letting me finish.
I want to learn what you do when you need cheering up. Mine is usually brushing a patient sheep.
Could we have friends over for a small meal? Small enough that I can learn where to put all the plates.
I have a spare button for your coat. It is the wrong color, but it is exceptionally committed to holding fabric.
I was worried about a loose rail all morning. Fixed it, then came to tell you the worry was gone.
We do not have to turn every walk into an errand. I am practicing that.
I like knowing which cup you reach for. It is such a little thing to get to know.
You can change your plans. I married a person, not a timetable.
The sheep at the ranch ignored my new haircut. Your opinion means rather more.
I put the tools away before supper. I wanted both hands free for washing up with you.
If I am restless tonight, it is a thought I need to untangle. You have not done anything wrong.
A good day is easier to recognize when I can tell you about it.
I kept the last apple for us to share. The knife is clean; I checked before sitting down this time.
I want to grow old with someone who still points out small birds. I think I chose well.
Come sit near me when you are ready. I have no task for you; I just like having you here.
I brought my work notes home, then put them away. I would rather hear your voice over supper.
You can remind me to rest without making a case for it. I am trying to learn that from you.
There is tea beside your plate. I checked its temperature with considerably more care than necessary.
I slept through the kettle boiling. Apparently I feel safe enough here to sleep deeply.
I love you. That sentence needs no qualification, and I enjoy that.
I have difficult days at the clinic. Coming home does not erase them, but it gives me somewhere to put my coat down.
Please tell me if you need comfort before advice. I am still learning to ask first.

I can warm my hands on a cup without catching a single fish. Retirement offers some efficiencies.
Snow melts on the water and disappears. I have spent whole minutes watching something so small.
The coast will be there when the wind is done. We need not go and supervise it.
I keep the old storm lantern clean. Today it is useful beside the chair, where I intend to remain.
Listen to the people in the room, if the wind troubles you. Nearer sounds can be a comfort.
Good light for finding a hairline crack. Poor light for pretending you did not notice it.
The deck is drying fast. I can finish one repair without dragging a damp cloth behind me.
That glare off the water could polish a spoon. I brought my hat for once.
I like this even light for checking paint coverage. The sun can be a flattering liar.
Cloudy weather makes the brass look quiet. It is still demanding to be polished.
I packed the rain cover anyway. Preparedness weighs less than a soaked toolbox.
I dried the tools before lunch. Rust would happily eat them while I eat my sandwich.
The boat cover sheds rain into exactly the place I wanted to stand. I admire its precision.
Wet rope needs room to dry. A tight heap becomes tomorrow's unpleasant discovery.
The boats are secured. Now we stay on land and let the knots do the job we taught them.
I tied down the loose gear before the gusts arrived. Saves the embarrassing exercise of chasing a bucket.
No repair needs me standing on a wet deck in thunder. The boat can file a complaint tomorrow.
I brushed snow off the cover before it grew heavy. Small jobs prevent large, soggy arguments.
Metal tools bite cold through thin gloves. I have exchanged dexterity for fingers that still feel present.
The shore looks new under snow. The slippery boards, regrettably, retain their old character.
The harbor checks are finished. I am accepting hot tea and refusing heroic ideas.
The wind can have the workshop door today. I secured it and moved my plans indoors.
We can draw a repair diagram while we wait. Paper is much easier to bring beside the stove than a boat.
The bright edge of every leaf makes the tree look embroidered.
I keep painting shadows too dark on sunny days. There is more blue in them than I first notice.
Sunlight on a white wall is not simply white. I could spend the morning trying to explain it with a brush.
This light lets colors speak without shouting over a bright reflection.
The clouds have a greenish gray underneath. Very faint. I promise I am looking at the sky, not feeling unwell.
A soft sky makes the distant roofs look like they belong to one another.
Rain darkens the path into a richer brown. My shoes are collecting quite a large sample.
I put the sketchbook inside my coat. The clouds can stay outside the paper for once.
The window breaks the view into drops. Each one holds an upside-down piece of the square.
I am drawing from indoors. The shutters make a dark border around the little light that gets through.
Lightning changes every color before I can name one. It is enough to have seen it.
I find the noise unsettling. Sitting near other people helps more than pretending I am absorbed in work.
Snow turns the shadows violet near the fence. I brought a pencil, which is a particularly inadequate response.
The roofline disappears against the pale sky until a bird crosses it.
I left some of the paper blank. Today the blank parts are doing most of the work.
The window is almost white. I am studying the warm colors of the room instead.
I have put my painting aside. Watching everyone share blankets feels more worth my attention.
The storm makes the lamplight seem close and solid. I am glad to sit inside that little circle.
Sunlight fades book spines. I have drawn the curtain exactly far enough to remain sociable.
The reading bench outside is dry. Please use it; otherwise I have oiled it for the benefit of pigeons.
A clear day is excellent for airing the map cabinet, provided one keeps an eye on the maps' escape routes.
Diffused light is ideal for examining old ink. Today I have an excellent excuse to delay the accounts.
The clouds resemble a diagram in our weather volume. Regrettably, it is the diagram labeled variable.
I brought a book to the window and discovered the window was already interesting.
A damp book should be dried with care, not hurried beside a fierce stove. I speak with painful authority.
There are cloths for wet hands by the desk. The books appreciate the courtesy even if they remain silent.
Rain makes the reading room popular. I am pleased, though I have had to retrieve three extra chairs.
I moved the oldest volumes away from the outer wall. Precaution is a remarkably good use of an afternoon.
Thunder interrupted my reading at a most appropriate passage. I shall resist improving the story with it.
The library is open for shelter. A book is optional, although naturally I recommend one.
Snow muffles the square. For once, my request for quiet has received meteorological assistance.
The records mention an old snow-clearing rota. The most heavily underlined instruction concerns returning the shovel.
I checked the window seals before the first flakes settled. Preservation begins with very ordinary chores.
We shall read indoors. Exploration can be conducted through an atlas with considerably warmer feet.
I have a list of neighbors already accounted for. Lists can be comforting when used for the right purpose.
The lamp oil is sufficient, and the kettle is full. That is the complete forecast for this room.
The bees are busy enough to ignore me. Good weather makes me a less interesting obstacle.
I watched three workers choose the same flower. There are worse endorsements.
Sun warms the hive wall early. I put my hand near it before deciding what work to do.
The bees take their time under this cloud. I see no reason to argue with them.
Flowers still have nectar when the sky is gray. People sometimes need reminding of ordinary things.
I planned a short inspection. The light and the hive's temper will decide how short.
Leave the hive lid alone in rain. A dry home matters more than my curiosity.
The bees are mostly inside. I checked the cover and let them keep their peace.
Rain on leaves sounds different beside the hives. You notice the missing hum.
I secured the covers early. Now the best work I can do is leave them secured.
No point opening a hive to prove I care. Keeping the weather out is how I care today.
The wind took a loose branch, but the hives are clear. I will deal with the branch after it settles.
I keep the entrances clear without making a fuss. Winter asks for a steady hand.
Snow around the hives looks quiet. There is a whole living warmth tucked inside.
Do not knock the boxes to see whether the bees are there. They have enough to do without answering visitors.
I checked shelter and stores before this blew in. Now I am trusting the work.
June says I can stop staring out the window. She is right. I dislike how often that happens.
The hives can manage with their covers secure. I am staying where Pip can find me.
We measured shadows this morning. Pip wanted to know whether a shorter shadow meant he had briefly shrunk.
A clear day is good for noticing shapes in leaves. You can learn a great deal without collecting a single one.
I brought the lesson outside and discovered the birds had prepared a competing lesson.
What do you notice when the light is softer? I find it easier to see the veins in a leaf.
We drew the clouds without trying to turn every one into an animal. That lasted nearly three minutes.
A gray sky leaves plenty of room for a bright question.
We set a jar outside to measure rainfall. Pip is concerned the roof is getting an unfair head start.
I moved the books away from the open window. Curiosity can observe rain from a dry desk.
Wet days are good for practicing careful observation. A puddle changes every time you look.
We are staying indoors and making a list of reassuring sounds. The kettle was everyone's first choice.
You may admit thunder startles you. Children learn courage better from honesty than from a performance.
I explained that we can help by staying where people know we are. That is a real responsibility.
We compared bird tracks in the snow from the path. The smallest prints made the biggest impression.
Snow gives us a chance to discuss what melts, what freezes, and why mittens should remain on hands.
I like a lesson that begins with everyone noticing the same beautiful thing.
Our lesson today is patience. We have warm drinks and several opportunities to practice.
Pip is helping fold blankets. A useful task makes waiting easier for small hands.
We can imagine an expedition from this table. The actual expedition will wait until we can see the path.
The leaves have turned their bright sides outward. An uncomplicated form of hospitality.
Sunlight moves across the shrine floor without hurrying. I have tried to learn from it. The kettle disagrees.
A clear morning is an invitation. It need not become an obligation to do everything.
The sky has lowered its voice. The birds have not taken the hint.
Clouds make the little lamps seem more awake.
I swept the steps beneath a gray sky. The leaves accepted the arrangement briefly.
The roots receive what the roofs refuse. Remember that when you empty a rain barrel.
Rain finds the hollow in every stone. I have placed a bowl beneath the hollow in my ceiling.
There is room beneath the eaves. Quiet company is welcome there.
The trees bend because they have somewhere to move. We should choose shelter just as sensibly.
I have extinguished the outdoor lamps and secured their doors. Reverence includes maintenance.
Thunder has enough to say without an interpretation from me. Come inside.
Snow rests on the old stones as gently as dust, with much colder intentions.
A white path asks us to slow down. The hidden step near the shrine asks more firmly.
The lamp glow sits warm against the snow. I checked the oil before admiring the symbolism.
The shrine will not resent your absence today. Stay where you are warm.
Some vigils are best kept beside a stove. I have excellent spiritual confidence in this one.
The wind is loud; the room is kind. Let us attend to the room.
My shadow can touch the fence before I can! Does that count as reaching it?
I found a beetle with a shiny back. It looks dressed for a very small party.
June says I need my hat. I think my hat needs a name if it is joining every expedition.
The clouds look like a sheep that forgot its legs. Do sheep dream about flying?
I drew the sky with my gray pencil. Now the pencil is very short and the sky is still enormous.
Hollis says the bees are waiting. I am waiting too, but I make more noise.
I found three puddles connected by a tiny river! I am watching from the path so my boots stay mostly boots.
My coat has a hood, but the rain still knows where my nose is.
June let me measure the rain in a jar. I am not allowed to add water to help it win.
That thunder was huge! I am sitting near June until my insides stop jumping.
My job is keeping the blankets folded. I made one into a square that is almost a square.
We are telling indoor adventure stories. Mine has a dragon who remembers to shut the windows.
I found bird footprints! They look like the bird was writing with both feet.
Can a snowball have a birthday if it only exists for one afternoon?
I made a tiny snow hill. It is a mountain if you are a beetle.
I am exploring under the table today. June says indoor explorers still have to come out for lunch.
The window looks like someone erased the outside. I know it is still there, though.
Hollis is here and June is here. I am making sure my wooden animals are here too.
Behold, a day made for the open road! After I repair this wheel's entirely ordinary squeak.
Sunshine displays my ribbons splendidly. It displays the dust on my coat with equal enthusiasm.
A traveler learns to savor clear weather without packing an unreasonable number of errands into it.
A silver canopy for today's trade! Free of charge, and regrettably impossible to fold into the wagon.
Clouds make polished trinkets modest. I compensate with my introduction.
The road is dry and the sky is gentle. My wheels require no grander blessing.
My wares are wrapped against the rain. My hat has heroically volunteered to collect the remainder.
A waterproof parcel is a love letter to one's future dry belongings.
I once sold umbrellas from beneath a leaking awning. Business was excellent; dignity was mixed.
The wagon is secured, and the grand expedition has become a modest visit to the inn.
I refuse to compete with thunder for attention. A rare professional concession.
Everything loose is tied down. I include my more ambitious travel plans.
Snow reveals every wagon track. At last, a record of my travels that requires no handwriting.
I brought warm scarves. Sensible merchandise can still have magnificent colors.
The road sparkles today. I admire it while watching carefully for the less decorative slippery bits.
My route can wait. A merchant who arrives tomorrow is preferable to a dramatic tale about today's departure.
I have spare blankets in the wagon's dry chest. Practical treasures, worth every inch of space.
We shall trade stories indoors until the wind exhausts its opening speech.
Clear conditions make the survey easier. They also make it harder to ignore how pleasant the valley is.
I took my lunch outside. No official purpose, although I initially attempted to invent one.
The boundary stones are plainly visible today. The gardens between them seem more deserving of attention.
Even light is useful when reading small markings. I am making good progress with the old maps.
The hills look closer beneath these clouds. My measurements disagree, quite properly.
I have brought a coat. Experience has cured me of treating an uncertain forecast as a personal challenge.
I wrapped my notes before leaving. Some observations ought to survive their weather.
The road surface changes markedly in rain. That is a practical matter a tidy plan can overlook.
I am waiting under the eaves. Please do not feel obliged to stand in the rain for my conversation.
Fieldwork is suspended. I can review figures without requiring anyone to search for me afterward.
I secured the equipment before coming in. Now I intend to accept the innkeeper's advice about tea.
The thunder is rather forceful. I would prefer to conduct the rest of this discussion indoors.
Snow obscures the markers. It seems sensible to acknowledge the limits of what can be read today.
I cleared the step where I am staying. A small obligation, but an immediate one.
The valley looks remarkably different beneath snow. Familiar measurements do not convey that difference.
There will be no site visits today. I have informed the people expecting me so they need not worry.
My report can be completed here. I appreciate the offer of a warmer chair.
I was preparing to check the equipment again. You are right; it is secured, and I should remain indoors.
Sunshine on the gate makes me think of all the mornings I left a chore for a walk. Sensible mornings, mostly.
I used to spread seed packets on the sunny step and call it planning. Mind the breeze if you try it.
Put your feet up for five minutes. The farm has survived longer pauses from me.
Cloudy light is kind to an old traveler. I can read a map without holding it at three different angles.
A gray morning still has birds in it. I have never needed the whole sky to be cheerful.
I packed a coat because I learned that lesson repeatedly and at some expense.
I remember where every roof drip used to land. I hope you have fewer buckets than I did.
Rain gives a farmer a little breathing room, provided the farmer does not immediately fill it with another job.
Take the wet coat off before telling your story. I want the whole tale, and that may take a while.
I have seen people confuse stubbornness with courage in weather like this. Stay sheltered and be stubborn about a crossword.
The loose things are secured. The rest of the afternoon belongs to the kettle.
A journey delayed is still a journey. I have learned to leave the road alone when it asks loudly enough.
Snow on the old fence brings back winters when I could find the gate only by knowing its squeak.
I used to keep a spare pair of socks near the stove. A modest habit with an excellent return.
The farm looks restful in snow. It is a useful reminder that growth does not have to be visible every day.
I have nowhere important enough to go in this wind. Pull up a chair and tell me how you are doing.
A stocked cupboard and good company make a fine destination. I am happy to have arrived at this one.
We can plan spring from here. The paper stays dry, and nobody has to prove they can find the far fence.
You came back to finish a difficult conversation. I noticed. That matters more than having the perfect words.
I found a note in the margin that disagrees politely with the author. Someone was reading with their whole attention.
You can be new at something and still bring useful experience. Tell me what this task reminds you of.
I saved you a place in my expedition drawing. You can choose whether you carry the snacks or the map!

sunroots.name: Under the Old Roots
sunroots.hint: Clear the orchard stump and boulder.
lines: The last stone rolls aside. Beneath it, a root holds a bead of sunlight as though the orchard has saved a little summer for you.

sunroots.name: Three Promises
lines: Three new trees stand on your farm. Here, the forest answers with a golden shoot: a small promise returned for three you made.

sunroots.name: The Patient Current
lines: You recognize the shadows beneath the current now. Between two smooth stones, a Sunroot bends toward the water without breaking.

sunroots.name: Salt and Soil
lines: A woven scrap from an old produce crate catches on the tide line. Under it grows a root whose warmth outlasts the sea breeze.

sunroots.name: A Place at the Table
lines: After the gathering, you help fold a tablecloth. A golden root has pushed between the square stones, exactly where everyone shared their food.

sunroots.name: Beyond the Headland
lines: The restored boat settles against the hidden shore. A Sunroot glows in the shelter of its rocks, waiting for someone willing to mend a way here.

sunroots.name: The Grove Remembers
lines: The lanterns stir above you. At your feet, one last Sunroot unfolds; its light feels like a hand resting gently against your own.

sunroots.name: Warmth in the First Dark
sunroots.hint: Explore the crystal chamber on mine floor 10.
lines: A thread of gold crosses the cool crystal. You cup it carefully, surprised that anything so deep underground can remember the sun.

sunroots.name: The Miner’s Pause
sunroots.hint: Explore the crystal chamber on mine floor 30.
lines: An old lunch tin rests beside a seam of stone. A Sunroot has grown through its rusted hinge, a quiet reward for stopping to look.

sunroots.name: Light Below the Mountain
sunroots.hint: Explore the crystal chamber on mine floor 50.
lines: The deepest crystal chamber hums softly. At its center, a Sunroot shines without flame, lending you strength for the climb home.
